genres.summary: Indo-Caribbean semi-classical vocal art of Guyana and Trinidad, root of chutney.

genres.name: Purahéi
genres.description: Purahéi, Guaraní for 'song', is the vocal, non-danced form of the Paraguayan polca, a slower 'polca canción' carried by voice with harp and guitar. Its bilingual lyrics in Spanish and Guaraní dwell on romance, nature, nostalgia and national memory, giving the buoyant polca a lyrical, song-centred face. It is a core strand of Paraguay's Guaraní-language song tradition.
genres.summary: Vocal 'polca canción' form of Paraguayan music, sung in Spanish and Guaraní.

genres.name: Compuesto
genres.description: The compuesto is a Paraguayan narrative-ballad tradition in which two singers, backed by guitar, harp, accordion and the rabel fiddle, recount a real dramatic, epic or tragic event set to the polca paraguaya or the rasguido doble. Structured in four-line coplas or ten-line décimas and sung in Guaraní or the mixed Jopará, it can memorialise a tragedy, satirise authority or praise a leader. It is Paraguay's storytelling counterpart to its dance and song genres.
genres.summary: Paraguayan narrative-ballad tradition recounting real events in copla and décima.

genres.name: Kaladja
genres.description: Kaladja is a traditional Creole couple-dance of French Guiana that weaves together the rhythms of grajé and kasékò, danced in single file with a gliding step known as grajé roumen. Once fallen out of use, it was revived by folk groups such as Wapa and is now performed across the territory's Creole dance repertoire. It is one of the secondary but cherished rhythms of Guianese Creole tradition.
genres.summary: Revived French Guianese Creole couple-dance blending grajé and kasékò rhythms.

genres.name: Chamarrita
genres.description: Chamarrita is a Río de la Plata littoral song-and-dance of Azorean-Portuguese origin, carried by immigrants to southern Brazil and settling through Uruguay into the Argentine province of Entre Ríos. Lively and swung, played on guitar, accordion and harmonica, it shows a clear rhythmic kinship with the milonga and gained its regional character with the accordion of later European settlers. It is a shared emblem of the trinational littoral.
genres.summary: Azorean-rooted littoral song-and-dance of Uruguay, Argentina and southern Brazil.

genres.name: Canto Popular Uruguayo
genres.description: Canto popular uruguayo is the socially engaged song movement that flourished in Uruguay from the mid-1970s, weaving native rhythms such as candombe, milonga and murga into acoustic, guitar-led song. Under the military dictatorship of 1973–1984 its concerts became rare spaces of gathering and quiet resistance, voiced by artists like Daniel Viglietti and José Carbajal. It stands as Uruguay's distinctive branch of the wider Latin American nueva canción.
genres.summary: Socially engaged Uruguayan song movement rooted in candombe, milonga and murga.

genres.name: Vals Criollo
genres.description: Vals criollo, the Peruvian waltz, is a coastal creole reworking of the European waltz that took shape in early-twentieth-century Lima, its lilting triple metre slowed and syncopated to fit criollo guitar and cajón. Felipe Pinglo Alva is regarded as its father, and Chabuca Granda later infused it with Afro-Peruvian rhythm and poetic imagery in songs such as 'La flor de la canela'. It is a pillar of Peruvian música criolla and one of the country's most beloved song forms.
genres.summary: Peruvian creole waltz, a pillar of música criolla shaped by Pinglo and Chabuca Granda.

genres.name: Landó
genres.description: Landó is a slow, sensual Afro-Peruvian genre in a rolling 12/8, built on the cajón and criolla guitar and prizing vocal expression and emotional depth over dance energy. Traced by ethnomusicologist Nicomedes Santa Cruz to African antecedents and kin to the Brazilian lundu, it is often seen within the genealogy that also produced the zamacueca and marinera. Revived through the twentieth-century Afro-Peruvian resurgence, it is central to artists such as Susana Baca.
genres.summary: Slow, sensual Afro-Peruvian genre in 12/8 built on cajón and criolla guitar.

genres.name: Yaraví
genres.description: Yaraví is a deeply melancholic mestizo song of the Andes, most associated with Arequipa in southern Peru, that fused the pre-Columbian harawi with Spanish troubadour song in the late colonial era. Usually in a slow 6/8, it dwells on sorrow, loss and unrequited love, and took shape in the picanterías and popular plazas of the highlands. It is shared across the highlands of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador.
genres.summary: Melancholic mestizo Andean song fusing pre-Columbian harawi with Spanish song.

genres.name: Pasacalle
genres.description: The Ecuadorian pasacalle is a spirited urban genre adapted from the Spanish pasodoble, built on an insistent ostinato bass and a marked, striding movement suited to street processions. Played by bands, it became the musical banner of Ecuador's cities and their foundation festivals, with pieces such as 'Chulla Quiteño' celebrating local identity. It blends Spanish popular form with Andean rhythmic and melodic character.
genres.summary: Striding Ecuadorian urban genre adapted from the Spanish pasodoble.

genres.name: Chigualo
genres.description: The chigualo is a montubio Christmas tradition of coastal Manabí in Ecuador, whose verses, close kin to the amorfino, are dedicated to the infant Jesus and sung in communal gatherings. In some coastal communities the term also names the wake held for a deceased child, blending devotion, coplas and unity. It is an intangible heritage of Ecuador's coastal peoples.
genres.sensitiveDescription: The Manabí chigualo is a montubio Christmas devotion to the infant Jesus and, in some coastal communities, a wake tradition for deceased children (velorio del angelito). Its religious and funerary dimensions are documented here respectfully from public sources and are not intended to reproduce restricted ceremonial material.
genres.summary: Montubio Christmas devotional song of coastal Manabí, Ecuador.

genres.name: Cueca Chilota
genres.description: Cueca chilota is the version of Chile's national dance native to the Chiloé archipelago, sung as a duet and played on guitar, harp, accordion and the tormento, a percussion box. Bound to community events such as mingas and boat launchings, it carries a rawer, more rhythmically driving feel than the central-Chilean cueca, coloured by the accordion brought by German settlers. It is one of Chiloé's most characteristic folk expressions.
genres.summary: Chiloé archipelago version of the Chilean cueca, sung as a duet.

genres.name: Vals Chilote
genres.description: Vals chilote is the waltz of the Chiloé archipelago, adapted from the European waltz that reached Chilean society in the mid-nineteenth century and reshaped by island custom. Danced with pronounced jumps and a tighter embrace over a strongly marked rhythm, it is more earthy and informal than its ballroom ancestor. Alongside the cueca chilota it is among the best-known dances of Chiloé.
genres.summary: Strongly-marked island waltz of Chile's Chiloé archipelago.

genres.name: Malambo
genres.description: Malambo is an Argentine gaucho dance-music of the pampas, dating to the seventeenth century, in which men duel through dazzling zapateo footwork over drumming and guitar. Purely rhythmic and competitive, it tests agility, strength and stamina, its rapid heel-and-toe patterns evoking the gallop of horses. It endures as one of the most virtuosic expressions of Argentine folk tradition.
genres.summary: Competitive Argentine gaucho footwork dance-music of the pampas.

genres.name: Vidala
genres.description: Vidala is a haunting folk song of northwestern Argentina, sung by a duet over the pulse of the caja coplera in characteristic 6/8-against-3/4 cross-rhythm. Undanced and meditative, it is built on the copla and on long silences, carrying an intimate connection to the earth and the Andean cosmos. It is among the most ancient-feeling strands of Argentine highland music.
genres.summary: Meditative caja-driven folk song of northwestern Argentina.

genres.name: Galerón
genres.description: The galerón is an improvised sung-verse tradition of eastern Venezuela, rooted in the Spanish décima espinela of ten octosyllabic lines and carried by bandolín, cuatro and guitar. Singers spin free-tempo counterpoint on themes from the sea and daily life to history, politics and religion, and it is the characteristic song of the region's Cruz de Mayo vigils. It is a cornerstone of the folk music of Nueva Esparta, Sucre, Monagas and Anzoátegui.
genres.summary: Improvised décima sung-verse tradition of eastern Venezuela.

genres.name: Polo Margariteño
genres.description: The polo margariteño is a folk song of eastern Venezuela, most emblematic of Margarita Island, sung in a moderate 3/4 or 6/8 over cuatro, bandola, guitar and maracas. Brighter than the galerón, it is often traded between two singers as improvised debate, telling of local customs, love and history. Together with the galerón it is among the most autochthonous musical expressions of Nueva Esparta.
genres.summary: Bright improvised folk song of Margarita Island, eastern Venezuela.

genres.name: Tizita
genres.description: Tizita is a melancholic Ethiopian and Eritrean song genre named after the tizita qeñet, one of the pentatonic modes of highland Amharic music. Its name means 'nostalgia' or 'longing', and the mode's yearning quality has led many to compare it to the blues or to Portuguese saudade. Rooted in older folk and Ethiopian Orthodox musical traditions, it flowered as a popular form during the 'Swinging Addis' years of 1960s and 1970s Addis Ababa.
genres.summary: Melancholic Ethiopian pentatonic song genre of nostalgia and longing.

genres.name: Azmari
genres.description: Azmari are the wandering minstrels of the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands, singer-poets comparable to West African griots or medieval European bards. Accompanying themselves on the one-stringed masenqo fiddle or the krar lyre, they improvise witty, allusive verses laden with metaphor, double meaning and sly social commentary. Their song is a centuries-old oral art still heard in the azmari bét taverns of Ethiopia's towns.
genres.summary: Improvising minstrel-poet tradition of the Ethiopian highlands.

genres.name: Kadongo Kamu
genres.description: Kadongo kamu, Luganda for 'one little guitar', is the oldest mainstream popular genre of Uganda, grown from Baganda folk song and oral storytelling. Built around a single guitar and voice, it prizes narrative over dance, its lyrics spinning witty love songs, moral tales and pointed commentary on current events. Pioneered from the 1950s by artists such as Elly Wamala and Fred Masagazi, it remains a touchstone of Ugandan music.
genres.summary: Narrative single-guitar song genre, the oldest mainstream music of Uganda.

genres.name: Kidandali
genres.description: Kidandali, from the Luganda word for a party or celebration, is a Ugandan popular genre that emerged in the mid-1990s as an evolution of kadongo kamu fused with the guitar language of Congolese soukous. Pioneered by the Afrigo Band, it began as live-band music before turning increasingly electronic and absorbing the dancehall and ragga rhythms popular across East Africa. It is one of the mainstays of contemporary Ugandan pop.
genres.summary: Ugandan dance-pop evolved from kadongo kamu and soukous in the 1990s.

genres.name: Kalindula
genres.description: Kalindula is a bass-driven Zambian popular genre named after the akalindula, a homemade bass instrument, and rooted in the Luapula-region dances of the mid-twentieth century. A neo-traditional style, it blends banjo, booming bass and stick-struck drums with electric-band arrangements in urban settings, its lyrics preserving folklore, custom and everyday life. It is one of Zambia's most distinctive national sounds.
genres.summary: Bass-driven Zambian neo-traditional popular genre.

genres.name: Burundi Royal Drumming
genres.description: The royal drumming of Burundi is a ceremonial ensemble tradition built on the sacred karyenda log drums, historically emblems of the mwami (king) and of fertility and regeneration. Drummers carry the drums on their heads in choreographed, physically intense routines of thunderous polyrhythm, a practice passed from father to son and dating back centuries. The Ritual Dance of the Royal Drum was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2014.
genres.sensitiveDescription: The karyenda drums of Burundi are sacred emblems of kingship, historically kept in sacred groves and played by ritual specialists for royal ceremonies; the tradition is inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. It is documented here respectfully from public sources and is not intended to reproduce its sacred or restricted ceremonial dimensions.
genres.summary: Sacred royal karyenda log-drum ensemble tradition of Burundi (UNESCO).

genres.name: Dhaanto
genres.description: Dhaanto is a Somali song-and-dance genre whose swaying movements are said to mimic the gait of camels, traditionally kept in time by handclaps and foot-stamping rather than instruments. Traced to the Somali region of the Horn of Africa and revived in the late nineteenth century by the Dervish movement to rally fighters, it has since become a celebratory national form carried into modern Somali pop. Its lilting rhythm has even been cited as a distant cousin of reggae.
genres.summary: Camel-inspired Somali song-and-dance genre, once a Dervish rallying music.

genres.name: Qaraami
genres.description: Qaraami is the classic popular song of mid-twentieth-century Somalia, an intimate, lyric-focused style built around the oud, voice and light drumming over a pentatonic base. Pioneered from the 1940s by figures such as Abdullahi Qarshe and the 'king of oud' Ahmed Ismail Hussein, it wove Arabic modal ideas into Somali melody, its love lyrics often veiling deeper commentary on politics and injustice. It remains cherished as Somalia's golden-age song tradition.
genres.summary: Oud-based classic Somali love-song genre of the mid-twentieth century.

genres.name: Haqiba
genres.description: Haqiba is the foundational popular song style of urban Sudan, a largely vocal art of poetry set to handclaps and light percussion that took shape in the 1920s and 1930s. Emerging as the secular successor to Sufi madeeh devotional chant, it filled weddings and gatherings and laid the groundwork for all later Sudanese popular music. Singers and lyricists such as Khalil Farah were central to its rise.
genres.summary: Foundational vocal-and-percussion popular song style of urban Sudan.

genres.name: Agbadza
genres.description: Agbadza is an Ewe music-and-dance of the West African coast, spanning Togo, Benin, southern Ghana and beyond, that evolved from the old Atrikpui war dance into a beloved recreational form. Driven by the gankogui bell, axatse rattle and a battery of drums, its sequence of movements ranges from an opening prayer to the ancestors to extended communal dancing. It is a centrepiece of Ewe festivals such as Hogbetsotso.
genres.summary: Ewe bell-and-drum dance of Togo and Benin, evolved from a war dance.

genres.name: Zinli
genres.description: Zinli is a Fon drum-dance genre of the Abomey plateau in Benin, created in the nineteenth century within the royal court of Dahomey and long tied to funerals and mourning. Its name comes from the zinli clay drum-vase at its heart, joined by gongs, rattles, handclaps and song. From the 1980s the artist Alèkpéhanhou renewed it into a celebrated popular form while keeping its solemn ancestral roots.
genres.sensitiveDescription: Zinli originated as a Fon funeral music of the Abomey royal court and retains a solemn, ancestral role alongside its later popular form. Its mourning context is documented here respectfully from public sources rather than reproduced.
genres.summary: Fon drum-vase dance of Benin, born as royal funeral music of Dahomey.

genres.name: Famo
genres.description: Famo is the accordion music of Lesotho, sung by the Basotho over accordion, drum and sometimes bass, and grown from the setolotolo bow songs of highland shepherds. It took shape in the 1920s as Basotho migrant miners carried their music into South Africa's mining towns, where it became a bond among men in the shebeens. Earthy and improvisatory, it remains a defining Basotho popular tradition.
genres.summary: Basotho accordion song tradition of Lesotho, born of shepherd and miner life.

genres.name: Socopé
genres.description: Socopé is a cheerful music-and-dance of São Tomé and Príncipe, one of the islands' signature Creole ballroom rhythms shaped by the meeting of African tradition and Portuguese social dance. Danced in couples to a swinging beat, it stands beside ússua and dêxa among the archipelago's most cherished cultural expressions. It reflects the plantation-era blending that defines São Toméan culture.
genres.summary: Cheerful Creole ballroom dance-music of São Tomé and Príncipe.

genres.name: Seggae
genres.description: Seggae is a Mauritian fusion of the island's Creole sega with Jamaican roots reggae, invented in the mid-1980s by the Rastafari singer Kaya (Joseph Reginald Topize). It marries sega's lively ravanne-driven rhythm with reggae's deep bass and relaxed groove, and its lyrics frequently voice social and political calls for unity. It became one of the most popular and identity-defining genres of Mauritius.
genres.summary: Mauritian fusion of Creole sega and Jamaican reggae, created by Kaya.

genres.name: Hira Gasy
genres.description: Hira gasy is a day-long open-air spectacle of the Merina highlands of Madagascar that fuses song, dance and kabary oratory into a single communal performance. Staged by costumed troupes, often related by blood or marriage, and sometimes as a contest between two groups, it carries moral, civic and cultural teaching to its audiences. Traced to the eighteenth-century court of Andrianampoinimerina, it was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2023.
genres.summary: Malagasy highland spectacle of song, dance and oratory (UNESCO).

genres.name: Kilalaky
genres.description: Kilalaky is a fast, frantic 6/8 dance-music from the Menabe region of southwestern Madagascar, rooted in the traditions of the Sakalava and Bara peoples. Punctuated by percussive breakdowns and built around the kabosy lute, it was modernised in the mid-2000s with keyboards, bass and drum kit while keeping its role in local ceremonies and festivals. It became one of Madagascar's most infectious dance crazes.
genres.summary: Frantic 6/8 dance-music of southwestern Madagascar.

genres.name: Intore
genres.description: Intore, the 'dance of heroes', is a Rwandan warrior dance-music historically performed by elite Tutsi military dancers and accompanied by an ensemble of ingoma drums and the eight-stringed lulunga harp. War-themed and once danced with real weapons to celebrate victory, it is now a centrepiece of national and family celebrations across Rwanda and neighbouring Burundi. Its hypnotic drumming and leaping, headdress-crowned dancers are among the most iconic images of Rwandan culture.
genres.summary: Rwandan warrior dance-music driven by ingoma drum ensembles.

genres.name: Kanmtole
genres.description: Kanmtole is a lively Seychellois dance-music, the Creole reworking of the European ballroom dances — contredanse, polka, mazurka, waltz and quadrille — that reached the islands in the early nineteenth century. Played on accordion, violin and banjo, it turns the old salon repertoire into a spirited, percussion-rich island form. It stands alongside moutya and sega as a pillar of Seychellois musical heritage.
genres.summary: Seychellois Creole ballroom dance-music on accordion, violin and banjo.

genres.name: Oviritje
genres.description: Oviritje is a popular music of the Ovaherero people of Namibia that began in the late 1960s as a cappella group singing and dancing at school and community gatherings. Built on tight vocal harmony, it later adopted keyboards and electronic production to become one of Namibia's most widely loved genres across ethnic lines. Its groups blend proverb-rich Otjiherero lyrics with call-and-response and synchronised dance.
genres.summary: Ovaherero harmony-vocal popular music of Namibia.

genres.name: Malipenga
genres.description: Malipenga is a competitive ngoma dance of the Tonga people of northern Malawi, born after the First World War when returning soldiers of the King's African Rifles inspired youths to imitate British military brass bands. Performers hum through gourd kazoos fitted with a mirliton to mimic the bugles that give the dance its name, marching in disciplined formation with prescribed ranks. It spread into Tumbuka areas and remains a highlight of community gatherings.
genres.summary: Competitive military-style gourd-kazoo ngoma dance of northern Malawi.

genres.name: Warba
genres.description: Warba is the great celebration dance-music of the Mossi people of Burkina Faso, centred on Ouagadougou and the Mogho plateau. Once reserved for the ritual enthronement and funerals of Mossi chiefs and led by the bendré calabash drum, it has become a joyous popular dance marked by vigorous hip-shaking and leg-lifting, today often driven by the djembe. It is among the most emblematic traditions of the Mossi court.
genres.summary: Emblematic Mossi celebration dance-music of Burkina Faso.

genres.name: Tende
genres.description: Tende is a Tuareg music built around the drum of the same name, made from a wooden mortar stretched with goatskin and played with pestles. Traditionally a women's domain across Niger and the wider Sahara, it pairs a female chorus with a soloist singing of village life, love and ancestors at camel festivals and evening gatherings. Its rolling rhythm is a foundation of Saharan musical life.
genres.summary: Tuareg mortar-drum music of Niger, traditionally led by women.

genres.name: Mgodro
genres.description: Mgodro is the signature traditional dance-rhythm of the Comoros, driven by drums, rattles and the gabusi lute over hypnotic, cyclical patterns. Performed at weddings, celebrations and religious gatherings, it blends Swahili-coast aesthetics, Malagasy timbres and Arab-Islamic modal colour, and it fused over time with the imported taarab of Zanzibar. It is one of the most recognisable island markers of Comorian music.
genres.summary: Signature traditional dance-rhythm of the Comoros islands.

genres.name: Sibhaca
genres.description: Sibhaca is a vigorous men's team dance of Eswatini in which barefoot dancers stamp and high-kick in unison while companions drum, chant and sing. Performed competitively for two or three hours at celebrations, teams are judged on precision and style, the dancers wearing colourful quilts and mohair leg-rattles. It is one of the most spectacular expressions of Swazi communal culture.
genres.summary: Vigorous competitive men's stamping team-dance of Eswatini.

genres.name: Zokela
genres.description: Zokela is a Central African 'modern traditional' genre that emerged in the early 1980s from the Lobaye region, named after its pioneering band and sung in Sango. It set electric guitars and drums to the ceremonial and funeral rhythms of the Lobaye, drawing on BaAka yodelling, the n'gombi harp and the montengene dance, with lyrics of social and political commentary. It turned a regional sound into a nationally beloved style.
genres.summary: Sango-language 'modern traditional' guitar-band genre of the Central African Republic.

genres.name: Tina
genres.description: Tina is a folk dance-music of Guinea-Bissau built around the tina, a gourd or water drum that gives the genre both its name and its distinctive beat. One of the country's core traditional rhythms alongside gumbe, it anchors village celebration with its binary pulse. It embodies the layered folk heritage from which modern Bissau-Guinean popular music grew.
genres.summary: Water-drum folk dance-music of Guinea-Bissau.

genres.name: Setapa
genres.description: Setapa is a traditional dance-music of the Bangwaketse of Kanye and surrounding villages in Botswana, its name derived from the Tswana for continuous stamping into the ground. Mixed troupes of men and women, dressed in animal skins and shell leg-rattles, stamp to the songs of a chorus, the men adding whistles and blasts on cattle horns. It is a defining Tswana communal tradition.
genres.summary: Tswana stamping dance-music of the Bangwaketse of Botswana.

genres.name: Bwiti
genres.description: Bwiti is the sacred initiatory music of Gabon, integral to the spiritual tradition of the same name that centres on the psychoactive iboga plant. Its polyrhythmic drumming, the mouth-bow and above all the sacred ngombi harp accompany night-long ceremonies of healing, initiation and communion with ancestors and spirits. Deeply woven into Fang and Mitsogo religious life, it is among the most profound musical traditions of Central Africa.
genres.sensitiveDescription: Bwiti is a living initiatory religion of Gabon centred on the sacred iboga plant; its polyrhythms and the ngombi harp are integral to ceremonies of healing, initiation and communion with ancestors. It is documented here respectfully from public sources and is not intended to reproduce its sacred, restricted or ritual dimensions.
genres.summary: Sacred initiatory ceremonial music of Gabon's iboga-centred Bwiti religion.

genres.name: Haul
genres.description: Haul (el-hawl) is the traditional art-music of the Sahrawi people of Western Sahara, sung in Hassaniya Arabic and organised around a system of modes. Its long poems narrate the land, epic and war, love, religion and daily life in call-and-response, and it was among the first Saharan musics to take up the electric guitar, influencing the later Tuareg desert-blues. In exile it became a powerful vehicle of Sahrawi national identity and resistance.
genres.summary: Modal Hassaniya art-music of the Sahrawi people of Western Sahara.

genres.name: Hipco
genres.description: Hipco is Liberia's homegrown hip-hop, rapped in Liberian English and the Kolokwa vernacular from which its name derives. Emerging in the 1980s and hardened through the country's civil wars, it carries an unflinching social and political charge, speaking against injustice and corruption in the everyday speech of Monrovia's streets. By the 2000s it had become the defining popular music of post-war Liberia.
genres.summary: Liberian vernacular hip-hop with a social and political charge.

genres.name: Tchinkoumé
genres.description: Tchinkoumé is a Fon popular genre of Benin whose rhythms descend from the funeral music zinli of the Abomey plateau. In the late 1970s Stan Tohon electrified it into the 'Tchink System', layering the traditional water-drum patterns with electric guitar, bass, synthesizers and a brass section drawn from soul, pop and rock. It became one of Benin's best-loved modern styles.
genres.summary: Fon popular genre of Benin, electrified by Stan Tohon from zinli rhythms.

genres.name: Akpese
genres.description: Akpese, widely known as Borborbor, is a social dance-music of the Ewe of southern Togo and Ghana's Volta region, created around Ghanaian independence in the 1940s and 1950s. Built on drums, the gankogui bell and brass-tinged highlife melodies, it is festive, participatory and closely tied to church and community gatherings. It is today one of the most popular social dances of the central and northern Ewe.
genres.summary: Festive Ewe social dance-music of Togo and Ghana, also called Borborbor.

genres.name: Marabi
genres.description: Marabi is the foundational township music of South Africa, born in the shebeens of Johannesburg's slumyards between the 1900s and 1920s. Played on pianos, pedal organs and later small bands, it fused American jazz, blues and ragtime with African melody into keyboard cycles that fuelled long, dancing parties run by 'shebeen queens'. It became the seedbed of South African jazz and of later styles such as mbaqanga.
genres.summary: Foundational South African township jazz of the 1920s shebeens.

genres.name: Ússua
genres.description: Ússua is a traditional couple-dance music of São Tomé and Príncipe, a stately Creole ballroom form shaped by the meeting of African tradition with Portuguese salon dance during the plantation era. Measured and elegant, it is led by a wind instrument such as a cornet and stands beside socopé and dêxa among the archipelago's cherished rhythms. It reflects the islands' distinctive Luso-African culture.
genres.summary: Stately Creole ballroom couple-dance of São Tomé and Príncipe.

genres.name: Damara Punch
genres.description: Damara Punch, also called ma/gaisa, is a popular Namibian dance genre grown from the traditional music of the Damara people and sung largely in Khoekhoegowab. Upbeat and guitar-and-keyboard driven, it turns Damara song and rhythm into a modern dancefloor style embraced across Namibia. It is one of the country's most distinctive contemporary sounds.
genres.summary: Damara-rooted Namibian popular dance genre, also known as ma/gaisa.

genres.name: Aghani al-Banat
genres.description: Aghani al-banat, 'girls' music', is a Sudanese women's folk genre performed at weddings and social celebrations, especially the bridal dance. Sung by professional women singers over the goblet-shaped daloka drum, handclaps and call-and-response, with playful lyrics of love and flirtation, it was pioneered by working-class and formerly enslaved women in Kosti and Khartoum. Its syncopated pulse became a foundation of modern Sudanese popular song.
genres.summary: Sudanese women's celebratory folk song genre built on the daloka drum.

genres.name: Mirskaawi
genres.description: Mirskaawi is a popular song style of eastern Libya, especially Benghazi, Al-Bayda and Derna, built on a well-known maqam. Traditions trace it either to the southern oasis of Murzuk, from which its name may derive, or to the Andalusian music carried by Moriscos who fled to North Africa after the fall of al-Andalus. It is a mainstay of Libyan festive and popular music.
genres.summary: Maqam-based popular song style of eastern Libya.

genres.name: Afar Music
genres.description: Afar music is the tradition of the Afar people of the Horn of Africa, whose homeland spans Djibouti, Ethiopia and Eritrea. Rooted in nomadic life and shaped by Ethiopic melody and Arabic modes, it ranges across marriage, war, praise and boasting songs, vocal games such as saxxaq, and prophetic adal songs, often carried by the flute. It is a cornerstone of the cultural life of Djibouti.
genres.summary: Nomadic Cushitic song tradition of the Afar of Djibouti and the Horn.

genres.name: Larakaraka
genres.description: Larakaraka is a courtship dance-music of the Acholi people of South Sudan and northern Uganda, performed at weddings and communal festivities. Accompanied by drums, harps, flutes and calabashes, young men display strength, agility and acrobatic leaps to win a partner, making the dance a celebrated rite of passage. It is one of the signature traditions of the Acholi.
genres.summary: Acholi courtship dance-music of South Sudan and northern Uganda.

genres.name: Sai
genres.description: Sai is a Chadian popular music that draws on the folkloric rhythms of southern Chad, brought to national prominence by the band Tibesti. Blending those southern traditions with the guitar-band influence of Congolese rumba and soukous, it became one of the country's defining modern styles. It carries Chadian song into a contemporary dance-band idiom.
genres.summary: Chadian popular guitar-band music rooted in southern folkloric rhythms.

genres.name: PNG String Band
genres.description: String band is the everyday popular music of Papua New Guinea, played on acoustic guitars and ukuleles by ensembles that often centre on a husband-and-wife singing duo backed by a dense wall of strummed guitars. It grew out of mission hymnody and the Hawaiian and Pacific guitar styles carried through the islands by traders, sailors and plantation workers, absorbing everything from blues phrasing to Southeast Asian pop along the way. The Paramana Strangers, formed in the 1960s, remain its most enduring name, and the spread of cheap acoustic guitars has carried the style deep into rural areas where it is sung in Tok Pisin and in local languages.
genres.summary: Acoustic guitar-and-ukulele popular music of Papua New Guinea.

genres.name: Singsing
genres.description: A singsing is a mass ceremonial gathering at which the clans and villages of Papua New Guinea each perform their own songs, dances and elaborate body adornment side by side. Hourglass kundu drums held by the dancers and great garamut slit gongs drive the massed movement, joined by flutes and the rattle of shell ornaments. Held largely between July and November, and staged on a huge scale at the Goroka and Mount Hagen shows, a singsing is at once celebration, competition and a public assertion of who each group is.
genres.sensitiveDescription: Singsing repertoire includes clan-owned songs, dances and adornments, and in some regions draws on initiation material and sacred instruments whose performance is governed by customary authority. This entry documents the tradition respectfully from public sources and does not attempt to represent its restricted or ritual dimensions.
genres.summary: Mass ceremonial gathering of song, dance and adornment in Papua New Guinea.

genres.name: Kaneka
genres.description: Kaneka is the Kanak popular music of New Caledonia, formed in the 1980s in step with the independence movement. It sets the tchap rhythm and percussion of bark, bamboo and leaves against the pulse and political stance of Jamaican reggae, adding rock and pop instrumentation and lyrics sung in Kanak languages and French. For a generation of young Kanak it became the means of declaring that they existed as a people after more than a century of colonial segregation, and it remains the territory's defining modern sound.
genres.summary: Kanak popular music of New Caledonia, fusing customary rhythms with reggae.

genres.name: 'Are'are Panpipes
genres.description: The 'Are'are people of Malaita in the Solomon Islands hold panpipe ensemble music in the highest prestige of all their arts. Players blow bundled bamboo pipes, called 'au after the bamboo itself, in sets tuned so that no one musician carries the tune: the melody appears only where the parts interlock, producing a dense, shimmering polyphony. The 'Are'are distinguish four kinds of ensemble and more than twenty named musical types, a body of theory documented in depth by the ethnomusicologist Hugo Zemp.
genres.summary: Interlocking bamboo panpipe ensemble music of Malaita, Solomon Islands.

genres.name: Vanuatu Water Music
genres.description: Known in the Mwerlap language as etëtung, water music is made by women of Gaua and Merelava standing waist-deep in a river or the sea and striking the surface with cupped and flattened hands. Arranged in a circle or half-moon and wearing flowers and woven armbands, they draw a surprising range of pitches and rhythms from the water itself, the beat travelling through the swirl each passing wave makes. It is now performed largely by the resettled Mwerlap community at Leweton on Espiritu Santo, which has carried it to international audiences since 2008.
genres.summary: Women's percussion tradition of Vanuatu, played on the surface of the water.

genres.name: Fatele
genres.description: The fatele is Tuvalu's principal dance-song, performed in the maneapa meeting house by anything from a dozen to a hundred people. Older men begin a song seated at the back; it is then repeated over and over, each time louder and faster, until the dancers in front are moving at full pitch and the whole house is carried along. The rhythm is beaten on a wooden box or an empty biscuit tin, and the melody and harmony bear the mark of the mission hymnody brought by Samoan teachers from the 1860s. It has remained exactly what it always was: a participatory act tied to real communal occasions.
genres.summary: Tuvalu's communal dance-song, accelerating verse by verse in the maneapa.

genres.name: Ura
genres.description: Ura is the drum dance of the Cook Islands, in which dancers tell stories through the hips and hands while a battery of wooden drums drives them on. The ensemble can run to ten players across pate slit drums, the smaller tokere, the double-headed pa'u and the large ceremonial ka'ara, hollowed from miro or tamanu wood. The dances speak of the ocean, birds and flowers as readily as of love and grief, and at full tempo the drummers lock together so tightly that a dozen players sound like a single enormous instrument.
genres.summary: Fast drum dance of the Cook Islands, driven by layered wooden drums.

genres.name: Kantan Chamorrita
genres.description: Kantan Chamorrita is the improvised call-and-response verse contest of the CHamoru people of the Mariana Islands, known to its practitioners as ayotte', to throw back and forth. Verses run to four lines, the second and fourth rhyming, and the closing line is hurled at an opponent who must build their answer around it. Sung unaccompanied at roof-thatching parties, feasts and by tuba-tappers working up in the coconut palms, it turned long labour into sport, and its whole art lies in teasing an opponent sharply without ever shaming them. Missionaries recorded clans competing this way as early as the seventeenth century.
genres.summary: Improvised CHamoru call-and-response verse duelling from Guam and the Marianas.

genres.name: Fa'ataupati
genres.description: The fa'ataupati is the Samoan slap dance, performed by rows of men who strike their own chests, arms and thighs, clap, and stamp in tight unison. It is the only Samoan dance that requires no instrument at all, because the bodies of the dancers are the instrument, and it demands both strength and exact timing to hold the pattern together. It is generally traced to the nineteenth century and to men beating mosquitoes from their skin, an ordinary irritation reshaped into a display of power and precision.
genres.summary: Samoan men's body-percussion slap dance, performed without instruments.

genres.name: 'Ōte'a
genres.description: The 'ōte'a is the fast drum dance of Tahiti, danced to percussion alone with no singing at all. Batteries of to'ere slit drums, cut from hollowed logs and struck with sticks, lay down a hard cracking pulse over the deeper pahu skin drum, and the dancers answer with a rapid shaking of the hips. Originally a men's dance paired with the slower women's 'aparima, it is now performed by both and forms the spectacular centrepiece of the Heiva competitions.
genres.summary: Fast Tahitian hip-shaking dance driven by to'ere slit drums, sung by no one.

genres.name: Lakalaka
genres.description: The lakalaka is Tonga's national dance and is best described as a sung speech: poetry, oratory, choral polyphony and choreography delivered as one thing. Men and women stand in long separate lines, sometimes several hundred strong, stepping briskly while their hands illustrate a text that recounts genealogy, history and the honour of a place. It developed in the nineteenth century out of the older me'elaufola and was sustained by royal patronage, and in 2003 UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
genres.summary: Tonga's national dance of sung speeches, recognised by UNESCO in 2003.

genres.name: Sāsā
genres.description: The sāsā is a Samoan group dance performed seated, by all ages and both sexes together, in long rows moving as a single body. The name means to strike, and the dance is built from crisp claps and sharp hand gestures that mime the work of everyday life: paddling a canoe, cooking, weaving, cleaning. A leader sets the beat on a rolled mat, a wooden drum or the side of a large tin, and the whole force of the dance comes from an entire village executing it in perfect unison.
genres.summary: Seated Samoan group dance of synchronised claps and mimed everyday gestures.

genres.name: Vude
genres.description: Vude is Fiji's signature popular music, assembled in the early 1980s from the rhythms and chant of traditional meke set against disco, country and rock and roll. The name carries the sense of floating on water, and the style is generally credited to Seru Serevi's 1980 album of that title, with Laisa Vulakoro so central to its rise that she is known as the Queen of Vude. It gave Fijian-language song a modern dancefloor idiom without letting go of its indigenous rhythmic base.
genres.summary: Fijian popular music built from meke rhythms, disco, country and rock.

genres.name: Aboriginal Contemporary Music
genres.description: Aboriginal contemporary music is the body of modern popular music made by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians, in which rock, country and reggae carry Indigenous languages, connection to Country and an unmistakable political charge. The Warumpi Band and Yothu Yindi brought it to national and then international attention, the latter setting bilma clapsticks and the yidaki against electric guitars and singing in Yolŋu Matha as readily as in English. Land rights, dispossession and reconciliation run through the songs, and the style remains the most widely heard Indigenous Australian music.
genres.summary: Modern Indigenous Australian rock, country and reggae in language and English.

genres.name: Waiata
genres.description: Waiata is the sung poetry of the Māori of Aotearoa, spanning waiata aroha of love, waiata tangi of mourning, oriori that carry genealogy to a child, and waiata poi. It is a vehicle for whakapapa, memory and proverbial wisdom as much as for melody. In the early twentieth century Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi shaped the waiata-ā-ringa or action song, which set Māori words to European tunes and added hand movements, among them the wiri, a rapid quiver of the hands evoking shimmering water or heat haze. Usually accompanied on acoustic guitar, it is now a pillar of kapa haka.
genres.summary: Māori sung poetry, including the twentieth-century waiata-ā-ringa action song.

genres.name: Jebwa
genres.description: The jebwa is the stick dance of the Marshall Islands, performed by men in coconut-leaf skirts and flower garlands who carry staffs and strike them together at set points in the choreography. A typical performance sets sixteen dancers against a handful of chanters and drummers, the hourglass aje drum played by women to support them. Once far more common, it is now reserved for occasions of particular importance.
genres.summary: Marshallese men's stick dance, accompanied by chanters and the aje drum.

genres.name: Ruk
genres.description: Ruk is the men's ceremonial dance of Palau, the counterpart to the women's ngloik. Chanting is the heart of Palauan music, and the texts sung in ruk carry history, place and clan knowledge passed down over many generations; body percussion and shouted group calls punctuate the movement and bind the dancers together. It belongs to feasts, village gatherings and the formal invitations extended from one village to another.
genres.sensitiveDescription: Palauan chant texts are frequently clan-owned knowledge, and the occasions on which particular repertoire may be performed are governed by customary authority. This entry is written respectfully from published scholarship and public sources and does not reproduce restricted repertoire.
genres.summary: Men's ceremonial chant-dance of Palau, counterpart to the women's ngloik.

genres.name: Micronesian Stick Dance
genres.description: The stick dance is performed across the Federated States of Micronesia, on Pohnpei, Yap and above all Chuuk, which is best known for it. Ranks of dancers sing while striking paired sticks against their own and their neighbours' in interlocking patterns, the clatter of wood serving as the percussion. Chuukese practice distinguishes the men's kepir from the women's tokia and sets both beside the marching lehp, within a wider musical culture that is overwhelmingly vocal and uses few instruments beyond sticks, conch shells and the body.
genres.summary: Stick-striking dance of Chuuk, Pohnpei and Yap in the Federated States of Micronesia.

genres.name: 'Aparima
genres.description: The 'aparima is the hand dance of Tahiti, its name built from apa, to mime, and rima, the hands. Gentle and lyrical where the 'ōte'a is fast and hard, it turns the arms and hands into a language in which each gesture is a word and each phrase a line of the story, supported by soft movement of the hips. The tales are drawn from fishing, weaving and daily life or from older myth, and the dance comes in two forms: the sung 'aparima hīmene and the wordless 'aparima vāvā, danced to instruments alone. Guitar and Tahitian ukulele usually carry the music.
genres.summary: Lyrical Tahitian hand dance that tells stories through gesture.

genres.name: Kailao
genres.description: The kailao is a war dance brought to Tonga from 'Uvea, or Wallis Island, in the nineteenth century. Men wield carved clubs known as pate kailao, whirling and clashing them in mock combat to the beat of a slit drum or a struck tin box. Alone among Tongan dances it is performed without any singing: instead the lead dancer calls out the name of each sequence and signals when to execute it, so that the dance becomes a demonstration of discipline, obedience and weapon skill.
genres.summary: Tongan war dance with clubs, danced without singing to a slit drum.

genres.name: Reigen (Nauru)
genres.description: Reigen is the term, borrowed from German, under which Nauru's traditional chant and circling dance repertoire is generally known. It rests on iruwo chants and iriang hymn-like songs sung in Nauruan, often in multipart choral harmony that blends indigenous practice with later mission influence, and on dances such as the slow frigate bird dance performed to a log drum. Much of the repertoire was suppressed after the German annexation of 1888 and further lost through the displacement of Nauruans during the Japanese occupation, but what survives is still performed at celebrations.
genres.summary: Nauru's surviving traditional chant and circling-dance repertoire.

genres.name: Sutartinės
genres.description: Sutartinės are the archaic multipart songs of north-eastern Lithuania, their name from sutarti, to be in concord. Sung mainly by women over melodies of only two to five pitches, they set a meaningful text against a refrain of nonce syllables, and are performed in close parallel seconds, in strict canon, or by paired groups trading phrases — producing a deliberate, ringing dissonance unlike anything else in European folk song. Nearly forty performance styles are documented, the tradition predates the Christianisation of Lithuania, and UNESCO inscribed it in 2010.
genres.summary: Archaic dissonant multipart women's songs of Lithuania's Aukštaitija region.

genres.name: Regilaul
genres.description: Regilaul, literally 'verse-song', is the old alliterative song tradition of Estonia, shared with the Finns, Livonians, Votes, Izhorians and Karelians around the Baltic. Built on a short repeating melodic line and a strict alliterative verse, it carried work, wedding, calendar and epic repertoire, and predates the Christianisation of Estonia in the thirteenth century. Widespread until the eighteenth century, it was gradually displaced by newer rhymed folk song and survived most strongly in Setumaa and on the island of Kihnu.
genres.summary: Estonia's pre-Christian alliterative runic song tradition.

genres.name: Rímur
genres.description: Rímur are the chanted epic poems of Iceland, performed in a practice called kvæðaskapur to fixed diatonic melodies. The verse form marries the end-rhyme of Latin hymnody to the syllable counting, alliteration and internal rhyme of the older skalds, and the narratives retell sagas, native legend and foreign romance, often at enormous length. They were the mainstay of Icelandic poetry for five centuries — hundreds survive from the eighteenth and nineteenth alone — sustained in farmhouses through the long winters.
genres.summary: Iceland's chanted epic poetry, sung to fixed melodies in the kvæðaskapur style.

genres.name: Faroese Chain Dance
genres.description: The Faroese chain dance is the national circle dance of the Faroe Islands and uses no instruments at all: dancers link hands in a ring and drive the rhythm with their own voices, chanting kvæði, ballads that can run to hundreds of stanzas with a refrain between each. The steps are simple, two to the left and one back, while a lead singer carries the narrative of kings, heroes and outlaws. Descended from the medieval European ring dance and banned elsewhere by the church, it survived in the islands' isolation as the only living European form.
genres.summary: Unaccompanied national ring dance of the Faroe Islands, sung to kvæði ballads.

genres.name: Spillemandsmusik
genres.description: Spillemandsmusik is the fiddle-led dance music of the Danish countryside, named for the spillemand, the town or village musician who played at dances, weddings and processions. The fiddle displaced older instruments in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries as chain dances gave way to couple dances, and the repertoire absorbed the polkas, reels and waltzes passing through Denmark's crossroads position in northern Europe. Distinctively, Danish fiddlers almost always play together rather than as soloists, giving the music its characteristic massed sound.
genres.summary: Fiddle-led village dance music of Denmark, played in groups rather than solo.

genres.name: Għana
genres.description: Għana is the folk song of Malta, often described as a meeting of North African and southern European sensibilities. It runs to three main forms: għana fil-għoli, sung by men in an extraordinarily high register without breaking into falsetto; għana tal-fatt, a narrative ballad recounting real local events; and spirtu pront, 'quick wit', the improvised rhyming duel that dominates today. Four or six singers trade extemporised verses over guitars, a prim guitar answering the voice between rounds, with invention prized above all.
genres.summary: Maltese folk song, best known for the improvised spirtu pront verse duels.

genres.name: Persian Classical Music
genres.description: The classical music of Iran rests on the radif, a repertoire of more than two hundred and fifty melodic units called gusheh, grouped into twelve modal systems — seven principal dastgah and five secondary avaz. Musicians spend years absorbing the radif from a master by ear, not as pieces to reproduce but as the vocabulary from which each performance is improvised anew according to mood and audience. It is carried on the tar and setar lutes, the santur, the kamancheh spike fiddle and the ney, and UNESCO inscribed the radif in 2009.
genres.summary: Iran's classical tradition, improvised from the radif across the dastgah modes.

genres.name: Bodu Beru
genres.description: Bodu beru, 'big drum', is the best-known traditional music of the Maldives, performed by fifteen to twenty people with a lead singer and several drummers. The drums are built from coconut-palm wood and headed with goat or stingray skin, struck with bare hands in a slow pulse that accelerates to a driving crescendo as dancers respond. Its roots are generally traced to East African communities who reached the islands as settlers and captives, their drumming blending with South Asian and Arab influences.
genres.summary: Maldivian hand-drum music that builds from a slow pulse to a crescendo.

genres.name: Baila
genres.description: Baila, from the Portuguese bailar, to dance, grew up among the Burgher and Kaffir communities of coastal Sri Lanka, descendants of the Portuguese colonial period and of Africans brought to the island. It is not an import but a Sri Lankan invention, fusing Iberian song forms with African rhythmic feel and local melody, given its lyrical modern shape by Wally Bastiansz in the twentieth century. It crossed every ethnic and class line to become the island's universal celebration music, heard at Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim and Burgher gatherings alike.
genres.summary: Sri Lanka's Afro-Portuguese party music, universal across the island's communities.

genres.name: Attan
genres.description: The attan is the national dance of Afghanistan, Pashtun in origin and traced back through pre-Islamic and Zoroastrian ceremony. Thirty to fifty dancers circle to the beat of the double-headed dhol, spinning faster and faster with scarves, handkerchiefs and sometimes swords, joined by rubab, surnai and flute. Once performed before battle to steel the warriors, it now marks weddings, births and national holidays, and is danced well beyond the Pashtun community across Afghanistan and into Pakistan.
genres.summary: Afghanistan's national circle dance, driven by the dhol.

genres.name: Zhungdra
genres.description: Zhungdra, the 'melody of the centre', is one of the two dominant forms of Bhutanese song, developed in the seventeenth century in the dzongs of the Paro, Thimphu and Punakha valleys before spreading village to village. It is marked by long sustained vocal lines that ornament a comparatively simple instrumental melody, giving it a slow, meditative weight, and much of the repertoire is attributed to saintly figures including Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, the founder of Bhutan. It is carried by the dranyen lute, the chiwang fiddle and the lingm flute.
genres.summary: Bhutan's ornate, slow-moving classical song form from the central valleys.

genres.name: Hsaing Waing
genres.description: The hsaing waing is the traditional orchestra of Myanmar, built around a circle of some twenty-one tuned drums with the player seated inside, answered by a matching circle of tuned gongs and led by the piercing hne oboe. It accompanies ritual, theatre, puppetry and festival, and its repertoire reaches back through the Burmese court — the earliest record places it in royal service in 1544 — drawing on Pyu and Mon antecedents. It shares much of its instrumentarium with the Mon piphat and the wider mainland Southeast Asian gong-chime family.
genres.summary: Myanmar's tuned drum-and-gong-circle orchestra, led by the hne oboe.

genres.name: Rara
genres.description: Rara is the street procession music of Haiti, taking over the roads each year from Ash Wednesday through to Easter. Bands walk for hours behind ranks of vaksin, single-note bamboo trumpets cut to different lengths so that players interlock one note each into a moving melody, joined by drums, scrapers and metal bells. Descended from the drumming traditions of the enslaved and shaped as much by protest as by celebration, it carries commentary on power and hardship into public space.
genres.sensitiveDescription: Rara is inseparable from Haitian Vodou: bands salute the lwa, and the season is understood by practitioners as ritual work carried into the street rather than as entertainment. It is documented here respectfully from public scholarship and is not intended to represent its sacred or initiatory dimensions.
genres.summary: Haitian Lenten street procession music built on interlocking bamboo vaksin trumpets.

genres.name: Gombey
genres.description: Gombey is the masked dance tradition of Bermuda, drawing together West African, British and Caribbean threads, its name from an African word for drum or rhythm. Troupes move to a mother drum carrying the main beat, side drums for the rhythm and snares trading call-and-response figures struck on both rim and skin, the dancers costumed in towering peacock-feather headdresses. It began among enslaved Bermudians granted a few days at Christmas, whose masks let them mock their enslavers unrecognised, and it was recognised as a distinct Bermudian form in 1970.
genres.summary: Bermuda's masked drum-and-dance tradition, born of Christmas festivities under slavery.

genres.name: Tumba
genres.description: Tumba is the carnival music of Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire, its name from the Bantu languages of the Congo and its roots in the music Afro-Caribbean islanders made during and after slavery. Sung in Papiamento and first carried by enslaved women as an outlet for grief — it is still called the Curaçao blues — it later took on merengue and Latin-jazz colouring and, in 1971, displaced calypso as the island's carnival anthem. The annual Festival di Tumba now chooses the official carnival song.
genres.summary: Papiamento-language carnival music of Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire.

genres.name: Jing Ping
genres.description: Jing ping is the traditional accordion-band music of Dominica, born on the island's plantations and named in imitation of its own finely textured sound. A band pairs the accordion with the boumboum, a bamboo boom pipe supplying the bass, the syak or gwaj scraper-rattle and a tambourine. It accompanies the quadrille and the circle dance known as the flirtation, and remains the music of rural festivals and community gatherings.
genres.summary: Dominica's traditional accordion band music, with bamboo boom-pipe bass.

genres.name: Big Drum
genres.description: The Big Drum, or Nation Dance, of Carriacou in Grenada is among the most direct survivals of African ancestral practice in the eastern Caribbean. Two boula drums and a cutter — Mama, Papa and Baby — underpin responsorial song and codified dance, and the repertoire names the African nations of origin outright: Temne, Igbo, Manding, Kongo and others. It is performed for tombstone raisings, marriages, boat launchings and in times of sickness or misfortune, calling on the ancestors to be fed and entertained.
genres.sensitiveDescription: The Big Drum is a living ancestral rite in which specific African nations are invoked and the ancestors are fed with song, dance and libation. It is documented here respectfully from public scholarship and is not intended to represent its ritual or restricted dimensions.
genres.summary: Ancestral Nation Dance of Carriacou, Grenada, naming the African nations of origin.

genres.name: Xuc
genres.description: Xuc is a Salvadoran genre and dance created by the composer Francisco 'Paquito' Palaviccini in Cojutepeque in 1942, drawing together indigenous Salvadoran music with Spanish, African and Cuban elements. It takes its name from the juco, a friction drum whose scraping call sounds like 'xuc, xuc'. Written deliberately as a national music for El Salvador, it spread through Palaviccini's own orchestra and his songs about the country's towns.
genres.summary: El Salvador's national dance genre, composed by Paquito Palaviccini in 1942.

genres.name: Punto Guanacasteco
genres.description: Punto guanacasteco is the declared national dance of Costa Rica, from the north-western province of Guanacaste. Couples circle in a flirtatious courtship dance, the women turning wide skirts while the men wave hats and shout bombas — short rhymed verses, often teasing — into breaks in the music. It is always carried by the marimba, usually joined by guitar, violin and singers, and blends Spanish, indigenous and African inheritance. Though treated as ancestral, its familiar form was composed by Leandro Cabalceta Brau.
genres.summary: Costa Rica's national courtship dance from Guanacaste, led by marimba.

genres.name: Benna
genres.description: Benna emerged among the newly freed people of Antigua and Barbuda in the 1830s, its name from a West African word for song-dance. Built on simple rhythms and call-and-response, its verses traded in scandal, gossip and sexual innuendo, and by the early twentieth century it had become a way of carrying news around an island where little else did. It gave the poor a public voice, and was eventually displaced by calypso, whose similar function made it easy to adopt as tourism grew from the 1950s.
genres.summary: Antiguan call-and-response song that spread news and gossip after emancipation.
